proposedTopics.title: Maximal Extractable Value (MEV)
proposedTopics.description: MEV is value a block producer (or those bidding for its ordering rights) can capture by including, excluding, and re-ordering transactions: PBS, the searcher→builder→proposer supply chain, and the sandwich/arb/liquidation strategies. Resources: https://docs.flashbots.net/

proposedTopics.title: Intents & ERC-7683
proposedTopics.description: Intents flip the model from 'sign an exact transaction' to 'sign a desired outcome and let solvers compete': the ERC-7683 cross-chain order standard and the UniswapX/CoW/Across solver markets. Resources: https://www.erc7683.org/

proposedTopics.title: Uniswap V4 Hooks (Deep)
proposedTopics.description: V4 hooks as first-class extension points: the beforeSwap/afterSwap (and liquidity) callbacks, dynamic fees, the permission-flag address encoding, and real hook design patterns. Resources: https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v4/concepts/hooks

proposedTopics.title: Restaking & EigenLayer
proposedTopics.description: How restaked ETH secures new services: AVSs and operators, the delegation/security model, slashing, and the EigenCloud verifiable-compute direction. Resources: https://docs.eigenlayer.xyz/

proposedTopics.title: Real-World Assets (RWAs)
proposedTopics.description: Bringing off-chain assets on-chain: tokenized treasuries (BlackRock BUIDL, Ondo), permissioned/compliant transfer designs, and the oracle/proof-of-reserve problem. Resources: https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/

proposedTopics.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs
proposedTopics.description: The concept-heavy strand: SNARKs vs STARKs, arithmetic circuits and constraint systems, writing a circuit in Noir, and verifying a proof on-chain. Math-heavy — stay conceptual plus one real build. Resources: https://www.rareskills.io/zk-book

proposedTopics.title: L2 Internals
proposedTopics.description: Under the rollup hood: Arbitrum Nitro's interactive fraud proofs, the OP Stack fault-proof program, and the sequencer/batcher/DA pipeline that turns L2 blocks into L1 commitments. Resources: https://docs.arbitrum.io/

proposedTopics.title: Proposer-builder separation (PBS)
proposedTopics.description: PBS splits block production into two roles: builders assemble a full, ordered block (competing on how much MEV+tips it pays) and the validator/proposer merely signs the most profitable header without seeing its contents until commitment. On Ethereum this is out-of-protocol via MEV-Boost + relays today; enshrined PBS is a roadmap goal. The point is to stop MEV extraction from centralizing staking, since a solo validator can outsource block-building. Resources: 📖 https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/mev/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/pbs.md diagram the proposer↔relay↔builder flow and explain what the proposer commits to (a header) before it sees the body. Done when: you can state why PBS uses a commit-reveal via a trusted relay and what a proposer could steal without one (unbundling/frontrunning the builder's MEV).

proposedTopics.title: The MEV supply chain: searchers, builders, proposers
proposedTopics.description: MEV flows through specialized actors: searchers scan the mempool/state for profitable opportunities and submit bundles (ordered tx lists with a bid), builders merge many bundles into the most valuable block, and proposers pick the winning block via a relay. Each layer bids up to the value it can extract, so most MEV flows to the proposer (and thus stakers) as priority payment. Resources: 📖 https://docs.flashbots.net/flashbots-auction/overview
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/mev-supply-chain.md trace one sandwich opportunity from a searcher's bundle through a builder to a proposer, labelling who earns what. Done when: you can explain why a searcher bids away almost all of its expected profit to win inclusion, and where the residual value lands.

proposedTopics.title: Flashbots & MEV-Boost
proposedTopics.description: Flashbots created a private orderflow channel: searchers send bundles to builders (bypassing the public mempool, so no frontrunning and no failed-tx gas), and MEV-Boost lets any validator auction its block-building to competing builders through relays. This democratized MEV access and reduced wasteful gas auctions, but concentrated flow in a few builders/relays — a censorship and centralization concern. Resources: 📖 https://docs.flashbots.net/flashbots-mev-boost/introduction
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/flashbots.md describe what a Flashbots bundle guarantees (atomic all-or-nothing inclusion, no public mempool exposure) and how MEV-Boost auctions a block. Done when: you can explain why sending a tx via a private relay avoids paying gas on a reverted arbitrage and why relay concentration threatens censorship resistance.
prerequisiteTitles: The MEV supply chain: searchers, builders, proposers

proposedTopics.title: Arbitrage & sandwich MEV
proposedTopics.description: The two canonical MEV strategies target AMMs. Arbitrage buys where a constant product (x*y=k) pool is cheap and sells where another is dear, re-pegging prices atomically for risk-free profit. A sandwich frontruns a victim's swap (buying first to push the price against them), lets the victim execute at the worse price, then backruns to sell — the victim's slippage tolerance is the attacker's profit. Resources: 📖 https://docs.flashbots.net/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/Sandwich.t.sol fork mainnet, seed a victim swap with high slippage on a constant-product pool, and script a frontrun+backrun that profits; then show a tight slippage bound defeats it. Done when: forge test proves the sandwich profits at loose slippage and reverts/ is unprofitable once the victim sets minAmountOut correctly.
prerequisiteTitles: The MEV supply chain: searchers, builders, proposers

proposedTopics.title: Liquidation MEV
proposedTopics.description: Lending protocols pay a liquidation bonus to whoever repays an underwater position's debt and seizes its discounted collateral. Searchers race to be first the instant a position crosses its liquidation threshold (often triggered by an oracle price update), frequently funding the repayment with a flash loan so no capital is needed. It's competitive, latency-sensitive MEV that also keeps protocols solvent. Resources: 📖 https://docs.aave.com/developers/guides/liquidations
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/Liquidator.sol write a flash-loan-funded liquidator against a forked Aave position and in test/phase09/Liquidator.t.sol drop the oracle price to make it liquidatable. Done when: forge test shows the liquidation repays debt, seizes collateral at the bonus, repays the flash loan, and nets a profit in one transaction.

proposedTopics.title: MEV-Share & order-flow auctions (OFAs)
proposedTopics.description: Order-flow auctions try to return MEV to the users who create it. In MEV-Share, a user submits a transaction with a partial 'hint' (not the full contents); searchers bid to backrun it, and the resulting MEV is split back to the user. This aligns incentives — the user captures value that would otherwise be a sandwich against them — at the cost of some latency and trust in the OFA operator. Resources: 📖 https://docs.flashbots.net/flashbots-mev-share/overview
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/mev-share.md explain the hint→bid→refund flow and contrast a user's outcome under a public mempool vs an OFA. Done when: you can state what a hint reveals and hides, and why an OFA reduces (but does not fully remove) trust compared with a private relay.

proposedTopics.title: Intents & solvers
proposedTopics.description: An intent is a signed statement of a desired end state ('I want ≥ 1000 USDC for 1 WETH by block N') rather than a fixed calldata path. Off-chain solvers compete to find the best execution route (across AMMs, private inventory, other intents) and submit it; the user's signature constrains the acceptable outcome. This moves routing complexity and MEV off the user, but introduces a solver-trust and settlement-guarantee problem. Resources: 📖 https://www.paradigm.xyz/2023/06/intents
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/intents.md write the difference between a transaction (imperative: exact steps) and an intent (declarative: constraints + outcome), with the solver's role. Done when: you can name what the user's signature must bound so a malicious solver cannot settle a worse execution than promised.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-7683 cross-chain intents
proposedTopics.description: ERC-7683 standardizes cross-chain intents: a CrossChainOrder struct plus a settlement interface (open/fill) so any filler can pick up an order on the destination chain and be reimbursed on the origin after proof of fill. A shared order format lets solvers serve many apps and chains instead of every bridge reinventing its own, improving liquidity and UX for cross-chain swaps. Resources: 📖 https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7683
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/erc7683.md map the ERC-7683 order lifecycle (user opens on origin → filler fills on destination → filler is settled on origin) and the fields that bind the fill. Done when: you can explain what stops a filler from being paid without actually delivering funds on the destination chain (the settlement/oracle proof).

proposedTopics.title: Solver markets: UniswapX, CoW, Across
proposedTopics.description: Three production intent systems: UniswapX runs a Dutch auction where the acceptable price decays until a filler takes it; CoW Protocol batches orders and settles them against a uniform clearing price, matching coincidences of wants peer-to-peer before hitting AMMs (MEV-protective by design); Across uses a bonded-relayer + optimistic-oracle model for fast cross-chain fills. Resources: 📖 https://docs.cow.fi/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/solver-markets.md compare UniswapX (Dutch auction), CoW (batch auction + CoWs), and Across (bonded relayer) on how price is discovered and who bears risk. Done when: you can explain how CoW's uniform clearing price protects users from sandwiching that a naive AMM swap would suffer.

proposedTopics.title: V4 beforeSwap & afterSwap callbacks
proposedTopics.description: A V4 hook is a contract the PoolManager calls at defined lifecycle points — beforeSwap/afterSwap and the beforeAddLiquidity/afterAddLiquidity family (plus initialize/donate). Inside beforeSwap a hook can adjust or skip amounts (via BeforeSwapDelta) and even take a fee; afterSwap runs post-execution for accounting. Hooks run inside the pool's lock, so they share flash-accounting deltas rather than moving tokens directly. Resources: 📖 https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v4/concepts/hooks
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/LogHook.sol implement a hook overriding beforeSwap and afterSwap that records swap counts, and test it against a v4 PoolManager in test/phase09/LogHook.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves both callbacks fire on a swap and the hook returns the correct selector (returning the wrong selector must revert the pool call).

proposedTopics.title: V4 dynamic fees via hooks
proposedTopics.description: A pool initialized with the dynamic-fee flag (fee == 0x800000) delegates its fee to the hook: the hook can update the LP fee at any time via poolManager.updateDynamicLPFee, or return an override fee from beforeSwap (with the OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG). This enables volatility-scaled fees, time-of-day pricing, or directional fees — logic impossible in V2/V3's fixed fee tiers. Resources: 📖 https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v4/concepts/dynamic-fees
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/DynamicFeeHook.sol set a higher fee when a swap pushes price in one direction and a lower fee otherwise, tested in test/phase09/DynamicFeeHook.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves two identical-size swaps in opposite directions are charged different fees, and the pool was created with the dynamic-fee sentinel.

proposedTopics.title: V4 hook permission flags & address mining
proposedTopics.description: Which callbacks a hook may implement is encoded in the low bits of the hook's own address: each permission (BEFORE_SWAP_FLAG, AFTER_SWAP_FLAG, …) is a specific bit, and the PoolManager reads the address to know which hooks to call. So you must CREATE2-mine a salt whose resulting address has exactly the right bits set — declaring a permission your address bit doesn't grant reverts. This makes hook deployment a mining step. Resources: 📖 https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v4/concepts/hooks#hook-flags
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/HookMiner.t.sol use HookMiner to find a salt so the deployed hook address has the BEFORE_SWAP and AFTER_SWAP bits set, then deploy via CREATE2. Done when: forge test deploys the hook at the mined address and pool initialization succeeds, and a version with a mismatched permission bit reverts at initialize.

proposedTopics.title: Building a V4 hook (Atrium patterns)
proposedTopics.description: Real hooks follow patterns taught in the Atrium Academy / Uniswap Hook Incubator: extend BaseHook, declare permissions via getHookPermissions, and keep hook logic gas-lean because it runs on every swap. Common designs are limit-order hooks, TWAMM, MEV-internalizing hooks, and oracle hooks — each must be careful not to reenter the PoolManager or break flash accounting. Resources: 📖 https://atrium.academy/uniswap
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: fork the v4-template into contracts/phase09/v4-hook and implement one non-trivial hook (e.g. a per-block limit-order or a fee that funds an oracle). Done when: forge test in the template passes for your hook including a swap that triggers your custom logic, and getHookPermissions matches the callbacks you actually override.
prerequisiteTitles: V4 hook permission flags & address mining

proposedTopics.title: AVSs & operators (EigenLayer)
proposedTopics.description: EigenLayer lets restakers extend Ethereum's economic security to new services. An AVS (Actively Validated Service) is any off-chain system that needs a decentralized, slashable trust layer — a data-availability layer, oracle, bridge, or sequencer. Operators run the AVS's off-chain software and are backed by stake that restakers delegate to them; the AVS defines the tasks and the slashing conditions. Resources: 📖 https://docs.eigenlayer.xyz/eigenlayer/overview
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/avs.md define, for a toy AVS (say, a signed-price oracle), what the operators do off-chain, what a task looks like, and which misbehavior is slashable. Done when: you can name the three parties (restaker, operator, AVS) and state what the AVS must specify for slashing to be meaningful.

proposedTopics.title: Restaking delegation & the security model
proposedTopics.description: Restakers deposit ETH/LSTs into EigenLayer strategies and delegate to an operator; the same stake can secure multiple AVSs at once, which is capital-efficient but means correlated slashing risk. The core tradeoff: pooled security bootstraps new services cheaply, yet an operator taking on too many AVSs can be slashed beyond what any single one bargained for, and shared stake can create systemic contagion. Resources: 📖 https://docs.eigenlayer.xyz/eigenlayer/overview
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/restaking-risk.md work a numeric example where one operator secures three AVSs and a slashing on one erodes the security assumptions of the others. Done when: you can explain why restaking amplifies both capital efficiency and correlated (systemic) risk versus each AVS bootstrapping its own token.

proposedTopics.title: EigenLayer slashing
proposedTopics.description: Slashing is what makes restaked security real: an AVS can, per its own rules, burn a portion of a misbehaving operator's (and its delegators') stake. EigenLayer's slashing framework requires unique stake allocation to an AVS's operator set and a safety/veto path to prevent buggy AVS code from wrongly destroying honest stake. Getting the slashing conditions provable and bounded is the hardest AVS-design problem. Resources: 📖 https://docs.eigenlayer.xyz/eigenlayer/concepts/slashing/slashing-concept
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/eigen-slashing.md describe how an AVS defines a slashable offense, how stake is allocated to that AVS, and what a veto committee guards against. Done when: you can explain why an AVS with a non-objectively-attributable fault condition is dangerous to restakers (subjective slashing).

proposedTopics.title: EigenCloud & verifiable services
proposedTopics.description: EigenCloud (EigenLayer's product direction) extends restaked security beyond consensus-style tasks toward verifiable off-chain compute and data: EigenDA for data availability, and verifiable AI/compute where results carry cryptographic or crypto-economic guarantees enforced by slashing. The thesis is that many web2 services could inherit crypto-economic trust without each launching a token. Resources: 📖 https://docs.eigenlayer.xyz/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/eigencloud.md pick one candidate service (DA, an oracle, or verifiable inference) and describe what 'verifiable' means for it and which slashing condition enforces honesty. Done when: you can distinguish cryptographic verifiability (a proof) from crypto-economic verifiability (a bond that gets slashed) for your chosen service.

proposedTopics.title: Tokenized treasuries (BUIDL, Ondo)
proposedTopics.description: RWA tokenization puts a claim on an off-chain asset on-chain. BlackRock's BUIDL and Ondo's OUSG/USDY tokenize short-term US Treasuries, paying yield to holders as new tokens or a rising price. The token is only as trustworthy as the legal wrapper and custodian behind it — on-chain code cannot enforce redemption of an off-chain bond, so these rely on regulated issuers and off-chain enforcement. Resources: 📖 https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/rwa-treasuries.md diagram the claim chain from an on-chain token back to the underlying Treasury (issuer, custodian, transfer agent) and where trust is required. Done when: you can name at least two off-chain trust assumptions that no smart contract can remove for a tokenized Treasury.

proposedTopics.title: RWA compliance & permissioned transfers
proposedTopics.description: Regulated RWAs need transfer restrictions a plain ERC-20 lacks: allowlists (only KYC'd addresses can hold), transfer hooks that check a registry, forced transfers/clawback for legal orders, and freeze functions. Standards like ERC-3643 (T-REX) encode this. The design tension is composability vs control — every restriction that satisfies a regulator also breaks a DeFi integration that assumed a free ERC-20. Resources: 📖 https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3643
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/PermissionedToken.sol implement an ERC-20 with an allowlist-gated _update/transfer hook and a compliance registry, tested in test/phase09/PermissionedToken.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a non-allowlisted recipient's transfer reverts, an admin can freeze an account, and you can explain why this token cannot be freely used in a permissionless AMM.

proposedTopics.title: RWA oracles & proof of reserves
proposedTopics.description: An RWA token's on-chain value depends on off-chain truth: NAV (net asset value) and reserve backing must be attested by an oracle (e.g. Chainlink Proof of Reserve) so the chain knows the collateral exists. This is the RWA analogue of the DeFi oracle problem — a stale or manipulated attestation lets a token mint or redeem against reserves it doesn't have. Resources: 📖 https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/proof-of-reserve
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/ProofOfReserve.sol gate minting of an RWA token on a proof-of-reserve feed so mint reverts if circulating supply would exceed attested reserves; test in test/phase09/ProofOfReserve.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves an over-mint reverts when the reserve feed is below supply and you can explain the trust you place in the attestor.

proposedTopics.title: SNARKs vs STARKs
proposedTopics.description: Both let a prover convince a verifier a computation was done correctly without redoing it. SNARKs (e.g. Groth16, PLONK) give tiny constant-size proofs and cheap verification but often need a trusted setup and rely on elliptic-curve/pairing assumptions. STARKs need no trusted setup and are post-quantum (hash-based) but have larger proofs. 'Succinct' = verify far faster than re-execute; 'zero-knowledge' = the proof reveals nothing beyond validity. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/zk-snarks-vs-zk-starks
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/snark-vs-stark.md tabulate SNARK vs STARK on proof size, verifier cost, trusted setup, and quantum resistance. Done when: you can state which property (succinctness vs zero-knowledge) a given use case actually needs and why a trusted-setup ceremony's soundness matters for a SNARK.

proposedTopics.title: Arithmetic circuits & constraint systems
proposedTopics.description: ZK proof systems don't prove programs directly — they prove that a set of polynomial constraints over a finite field is satisfied. You express a computation as an arithmetic circuit (additions and multiplications over field elements), compiled into a constraint system (R1CS for Groth16, or PLONKish gates). A 'witness' is a valid assignment to all wires; the proof shows the prover knows one without revealing it. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/post/arithmetic-circuit
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/circuits.md express a small statement ('I know x such that x^3 + x + 5 == 35') as arithmetic constraints and identify the public vs private (witness) signals. Done when: you can explain why every operation must be reduced to add/multiply gates over a finite field and what the witness contains vs what the verifier sees.

proposedTopics.title: Writing a Noir circuit
proposedTopics.description: Noir (Aztec) is a Rust-like DSL for writing ZK circuits without hand-rolling constraints: you write a `main` with `pub` (public) and private inputs plus `assert` constraints, and `nargo` compiles it and generates/verifies proofs. Noir abstracts the proving backend so the same circuit can target different systems. It's the most approachable on-ramp to actually shipping a proof. Resources: 📖 https://noir-lang.org/docs
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/noir/ install nargo and write a circuit proving knowledge of a preimage (assert hash(x) == public_hash) or that a private value is in a range; run `nargo prove` and `nargo verify`. Done when: nargo verifies a proof for a correct witness and rejects a wrong one, and you can point to which inputs are public vs private in your main.

proposedTopics.title: On-chain ZK verifiers
proposedTopics.description: To use a proof on Ethereum you deploy a verifier contract (often auto-generated by the toolchain, e.g. from Noir/snarkjs) exposing verify(proof, publicInputs) → bool. It runs the pairing/hash checks in the EVM — cheap for a SNARK (a few hundred k gas via the ecPairing precompile), heavier for a STARK. The contract trusts the verification key baked in at deploy time, so a wrong or malicious key breaks soundness. Resources: 📖 https://www.rareskills.io/zk-book
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/verifier generate a Solidity verifier from your Noir circuit and call it in test/phase09/Verifier.t.sol with a real proof + public inputs. Done when: forge test proves verify() returns true for a valid proof and false for a tampered one, and you can identify where the verification key lives.

proposedTopics.title: ZK applications: rollups, privacy, identity
proposedTopics.description: ZK proofs unlock three families: validity (ZK) rollups prove a batch of L2 execution to L1 for near-instant finality; privacy apps (mixers, private payments, private voting) prove a statement without revealing inputs; and identity/compliance proofs (proof of humanity, proof of age, KYC without doxxing) reveal a predicate instead of the data. The shared idea: prove a fact, hide the witness. Resources: 📖 https://ethereum.org/en/zero-knowledge-proofs/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/zk-apps.md pick one application (rollup, private transfer, or selective-disclosure identity) and specify its public inputs, private witness, and the statement being proven. Done when: you can articulate, for your chosen app, exactly what stays private and what a verifier learns.

proposedTopics.title: Arbitrum Nitro & interactive fraud proofs
proposedTopics.description: Nitro compiles the L2 state-transition function to WASM (WAVM) and settles disputes with an interactive fraud proof: a challenged assertion is bisected round by round until the disagreement narrows to a single WAVM instruction, which L1 then executes to decide who is right. This 'one-step proof' means L1 only ever re-runs one instruction, not the whole batch — cheap on-chain, but requiring an honest challenger within the window. Resources: 📖 https://docs.arbitrum.io/how-arbitrum-works/fraud-proofs/challenge-manager
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/nitro-fraud.md walk through the bisection game: assertion → dissection rounds → one-step proof, naming what L1 executes. Done when: you can explain why interactive fraud proofs keep L1 cost near-constant regardless of batch size and why liveness of at least one honest challenger is required.

proposedTopics.title: OP Stack & fault proofs
proposedTopics.description: The OP Stack's fault-proof system pairs a fault-proof program (FPP — the deterministic L2 state transition, runnable off-chain) with a fault-proof VM (FPVM, e.g. Cannon/MIPS) so a disputed output can be re-derived and bisected on L1. Its permissionless fault proofs and modular design (rollup node, batcher, proposer) underpin the Superchain of OP-based chains sharing a standard. Resources: 📖 https://docs.optimism.io/stack/fault-proofs/explainer
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/op-stack.md diagram the OP Stack components (rollup node, batcher, proposer, fault-proof program + VM) and how a disputed output root is challenged. Done when: you can explain the role of the fault-proof program vs the fault-proof VM and why a shared standard enables the Superchain.

proposedTopics.title: Sequencer, batcher & data availability
proposedTopics.description: A rollup's pipeline: the sequencer orders L2 transactions and issues fast soft-confirmations; the batcher compresses batches and posts them to L1 (as EIP-4844 blobs) for data availability; and a proposer posts state/output roots. DA is the security linchpin — if batch data isn't actually published, no one can reconstruct L2 state or prove fraud, so 'the data must be available' is what separates a real rollup from a validium. Resources: 📖 https://docs.arbitrum.io/how-arbitrum-works/sequencer
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase09/l2-pipeline.md trace an L2 tx from sequencer soft-confirm → batcher blob post → L1 finality, marking where DA is guaranteed. Done when: you can explain why posting batch data to L1 (not just a state root) is what lets anyone challenge fraud, and how a validium weakens this.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does PBS separate, and what does the proposer actually commit to?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Builders assemble ordered blocks and compete on total value; the proposer signs only the most profitable header (blind to the body until commitment), today via MEV-Boost + relays. Pitfall: without a trusted relay's commit-reveal, a proposer could unbundle and steal the builder's MEV — PBS exists partly to stop MEV from centralizing staking.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: The MEV supply chain: searchers, builders, proposers
proposedPrompts.promptText: Trace MEV through its actors and say where most of the value ends up.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Searchers find opportunities and submit bundles with a bid → builders merge bundles into the most valuable block → proposers pick the winning block via a relay. Competition bids most value up to the proposer (stakers). Pitfall: a searcher must bid away nearly all expected profit to win inclusion, so being marginally faster/smarter is the whole edge.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does sending a bundle through Flashbots (vs the public mempool) give you, and what's the systemic cost?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A private channel: atomic all-or-nothing bundle inclusion, no public-mempool frontrunning, and no gas paid on reverted arbs; MEV-Boost auctions block-building to competing builders. Pitfall: flow concentrates in a few builders/relays, creating a censorship and centralization vector.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a sandwich attack profit, and what defeats it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Frontrun the victim's swap to push price against them, let them execute at the worse price, backrun to sell — their slippage tolerance is your profit. A tight minAmountOut (slippage bound) makes the victim's tx revert before it can be exploited. Pitfall: setting slippage too loose (or infinite) on a constant-product pool is what makes you sandwichable.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why do searchers race to liquidate, and how do they need no capital?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Repaying an underwater position's debt earns a liquidation bonus on the seized discounted collateral; the trigger is often an oracle price update, so it's a first-come latency race. A flash loan funds the repayment and is repaid within the same tx from the seized collateral. Pitfall: liquidation MEV is competitive but also what keeps lending protocols solvent.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Practice building a flash-loan-funded liquidation bot (Damn Vulnerable DeFi puppet-style / real Aave).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Flash-borrow the debt asset, repay the position, seize discounted collateral, swap enough to repay the loan, keep the bonus — all atomic.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does an order-flow auction return MEV to users?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The user submits a tx with a partial hint; searchers bid to backrun it and the resulting MEV is split back to the user, capturing value a sandwich would otherwise steal. Pitfall: it reduces but doesn't remove trust — you still rely on the OFA operator, and the hint leaks some information at some latency cost.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does an intent differ from a transaction, and what must the signature bound?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A transaction is imperative (exact calldata/steps); an intent is declarative (a signed outcome + constraints) that solvers compete to fill. The signature must bound the acceptable result (min output, deadline, chains). Pitfall: if the intent under-constrains the outcome, a malicious solver can settle a worse execution and pocket the difference.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does ERC-7683 standardize, and what protects the origin-chain payer?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A CrossChainOrder struct + open/fill settlement interface so any filler can serve an order on the destination chain and be reimbursed on the origin. A settlement proof/oracle of the destination fill is what stops a filler from being paid without delivering. Pitfall: the security reduces to the correctness of that cross-chain settlement proof.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Contrast UniswapX, CoW, and Across on price discovery and risk.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: UniswapX = Dutch auction (price decays until a filler takes it); CoW = batch auction with a uniform clearing price and peer-to-peer coincidence-of-wants matching before AMMs; Across = bonded relayer + optimistic oracle for fast cross-chain fills. Pitfall: CoW's uniform clearing price is what structurally prevents intra-batch sandwiching a naive AMM swap would suffer.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do V4's swap hooks fire, and what must a hook return?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: beforeSwap runs before the swap (can adjust amounts via BeforeSwapDelta or take a fee) and afterSwap runs after, both inside the pool's lock sharing flash-accounting deltas. Each callback must return its exact function selector. Pitfall: returning the wrong selector (or reentering the PoolManager) reverts the pool call — the selector return is the PoolManager's safety check.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a V4 pool get a dynamic fee?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Initialize the pool with the dynamic-fee sentinel (fee == 0x800000); the hook then sets the LP fee via updateDynamicLPFee or returns an override fee from beforeSwap (OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG), enabling volatility- or direction-scaled fees. Pitfall: a pool created with a fixed fee can never become dynamic — the flag is set at initialization, not later.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: V4 hook permission flags & address mining
proposedPrompts.promptText: How does the PoolManager know which hooks to call, and why must you mine the hook address?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The permitted callbacks are encoded in the low bits of the hook's own address (BEFORE_SWAP_FLAG, AFTER_SWAP_FLAG, …); the PoolManager reads the address. So you CREATE2-mine a salt giving an address with exactly the needed bits. Pitfall: declaring a permission whose address bit isn't set (or vice versa) reverts at pool initialization.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What must a production V4 hook get right, and why is gas-leanness non-negotiable?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Extend BaseHook, declare permissions via getHookPermissions that exactly match the callbacks you override, and keep logic cheap because the hook runs on every swap; common designs are limit orders, TWAMM, oracle, and MEV-internalizing hooks. Pitfall: reentering the PoolManager or mismatching getHookPermissions against your address's flag bits breaks flash accounting or reverts pool init.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Build and test a Uniswap V4 hook from the official template (Hook Incubator style).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Extend BaseHook, implement getHookPermissions + the callbacks you need, mine the address, and prove a swap triggers your logic in the v4-template test harness.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is an AVS, and who are the three parties in EigenLayer?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An AVS (Actively Validated Service) is any off-chain system needing decentralized, slashable trust (DA, oracle, bridge, sequencer); operators run its software backed by stake that restakers delegate. Pitfall: slashing is only meaningful if the AVS specifies an objectively attributable fault condition — otherwise stake can be destroyed subjectively.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is the core tradeoff of restaking the same stake across many AVSs?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Pooled/reused stake bootstraps new services cheaply (capital efficiency) but creates correlated slashing and systemic contagion — an operator over-committed across AVSs can be slashed beyond what any one AVS assumed. Pitfall: shared stake means one AVS's failure can erode the security other AVSs were relying on.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does EigenLayer's slashing framework require to protect honest restakers?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Unique stake allocation to an AVS's operator set plus a safety/veto path, so a buggy AVS can't wrongly burn honest stake; the AVS must define objectively attributable, bounded slashing conditions. Pitfall: an AVS with subjective (non-attributable) fault conditions is dangerous — honest operators could be slashed for disputes they can't prove they won.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What distinguishes cryptographic from crypto-economic verifiability for an EigenCloud service?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Cryptographic verifiability means the result carries a proof anyone can check (e.g. a validity proof); crypto-economic means honesty is enforced by a bond that gets slashed on detected misbehavior. Pitfall: crypto-economic guarantees are only as strong as the stake at risk and the ability to detect + attribute the fault.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is a tokenized Treasury only as safe as its off-chain wrapper?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The token is a claim on an off-chain bond held by a custodian; on-chain code can't force redemption or prove the asset exists, so trust rests on the regulated issuer, custodian, and transfer agent. Pitfall: 'on-chain' doesn't mean trustless here — the hardest failure modes (custody, redemption, legal) live entirely off-chain.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What must a compliant RWA token add over a plain ERC-20, and what does it break?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Allowlist-gated transfers, a compliance registry/transfer hook, forced transfer/clawback, and freeze (via ERC-3643/ERC-1400). Pitfall: every restriction that satisfies a regulator also breaks permissionless composability — such a token can't be dropped into an open AMM that assumes a free ERC-20.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why do RWAs need proof-of-reserve oracles, and what's the residual trust?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: On-chain value depends on off-chain reserves/NAV, so an attested feed (e.g. Chainlink Proof of Reserve) must confirm backing before mint/redeem; a stale or manipulated attestation lets a token mint against reserves it lacks. Pitfall: this only moves trust to the attestor — it's the RWA version of the DeFi oracle problem.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Contrast SNARKs and STARKs on setup, proof size, and quantum resistance.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: SNARKs: tiny proofs, cheap verification, but often a trusted setup and pairing-based (not post-quantum). STARKs: no trusted setup and post-quantum (hash-based), but larger proofs. Both are succinct (verify << re-execute). Pitfall: a SNARK's soundness depends on its trusted-setup ceremony — if the toxic waste leaks, fake proofs become possible.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What do ZK systems actually prove, and what is the witness?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: That a set of polynomial constraints over a finite field is satisfied — the computation is compiled to an arithmetic circuit (add/multiply gates) and then a constraint system (R1CS / PLONKish). The witness is a valid assignment to all wires; the proof shows the prover knows one without revealing it. Pitfall: everything must reduce to field add/multiply — no native branching or unbounded loops.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In a Noir `main`, what distinguishes public from private inputs, and how do you verify?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Inputs marked `pub` are public (seen by the verifier); unmarked inputs are private witness; `assert` statements are the constraints. `nargo prove` generates a proof from a witness and `nargo verify` checks it. Pitfall: anything not marked `pub` stays hidden — leaking a value means marking it public by mistake.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write and prove a Noir circuit for a hash preimage, then verify it.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: main(x: Field, pub h: Field) { assert(hash(x) == h); } — nargo prove with a correct x, nargo verify accepts; a wrong x fails to prove.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does an on-chain SNARK verifier work, and where is its trust anchored?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A deployed verifier exposes verify(proof, publicInputs) and runs the pairing checks via the ecPairing precompile (a few hundred k gas); it trusts the verification key baked in at deploy time. Pitfall: a wrong or malicious verification key breaks soundness invisibly — the contract will 'verify' proofs for a different circuit.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Across ZK rollups, privacy apps, and identity proofs, what is the common pattern?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Prove a fact while hiding the witness: rollups prove correct L2 execution to L1 (validity), privacy apps prove a statement without revealing inputs, identity proofs reveal a predicate (over 18, is human) not the data. Pitfall: define public inputs vs private witness precisely — a value accidentally made public defeats the privacy goal.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a Nitro interactive fraud proof keep L1 cost low?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A challenged assertion is bisected round by round until the dispute is a single WAVM instruction, which L1 then executes (the one-step proof) to decide the winner — L1 never re-runs the whole batch. Pitfall: it requires at least one honest challenger online within the challenge window; without one, a false assertion finalizes.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What are the two halves of the OP Stack fault-proof system?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The fault-proof program (FPP) — the deterministic L2 state transition, runnable off-chain — and the fault-proof VM (FPVM, e.g. Cannon/MIPS) that re-executes and bisects a disputed output on L1. Pitfall: a shared, standardized fault-proof + component set is what lets many OP chains form the interoperable Superchain.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is data availability, not the state root, the security linchpin of a rollup?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The sequencer orders txs and the batcher posts the compressed batch data to L1 (as blobs); if that data isn't actually published, no one can reconstruct L2 state or prove fraud. Pitfall: a validium posts only a state root and keeps data off-chain — weakening exactly this guarantee, so it isn't a full rollup.
